summary: Flame Atlas turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into a fire-safety tool for crewed habitats. It reads all 24 combustion investigations in NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), merges their 22 experiment tables into one table of 1,872 individual tests in common units, and lets an engineer describe a crew environment (oxygen, pressure, gravity, airflow, fuel) to see which investigations tested conditions closest to it, with an open score and a source for every value. It also makes the gaps visible: of all those tests, only 20 were run in the oxygen-enriched, low-pressure atmosphere planned for lunar and Mars habitats, all of them gas-burner flames, and no solid material was tested above 22.7 % oxygen. Knowing what has not been tested matters for fire safety as much as knowing what has. SI (a language model) reads NASA's tables, test matrices and operator notes into that one table and writes a short brief that interprets each preset environment; code checks every value it reads and every number it writes against the NASA source, and shows the source next to it.
details:
The problem

Lunar and Mars habitat concepts plan an oxygen-enriched, reduced-pressure atmosphere: at least 30 % oxygen at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psi) or less, in partial gravity. Materials burn differently there than in an ISS cabin, and a crew cannot leave. NASA has run 24 combustion investigations that bear on this, but their results sit in 22 tables with different columns and units and in hundreds of documents. Nobody can ask them one question.

What it does

  • Scenario. Choose a preset (ISS cabin, lunar or Mars habitat, pressurized rover, EVA suit) or enter your own oxygen, pressure, gravity, airflow, fuel state and fire-safety focus. The screen shows how many tests with that fuel were run near the environment, sets the environment beside the range NASA actually tested, and ranks the 24 investigations by how close their test conditions are. Every score is broken into seven parts, and the card shows its closest tests and how many of the 100 points could be checked against data. For a preset, an SI brief puts these numbers into a few sentences; code checks every number and investigation name in it, and "What was checked" lists the facts behind each sentence.
  • Tests. One table of 1,989 rows (1,872 individual tests plus test-day and test-matrix summaries) from 22 NASA tables. Filter by investigation, fuel state, oxygen, pressure, airflow, row type and outcome; export to CSV or JSON for modelling. Every row opens its NASA file, row number, original cells and the notes that quote the NASA document a value came from. The outcome of 75 BASS tests, read by SI from the operators' notes, carries an SI mark and its quote.
  • Coverage. A grid of oxygen against pressure or airflow with the number of tests in each cell, the exploration atmosphere marked, and the data gaps counted. Each count opens exactly the rows it counted.
  • Investigations. A card per investigation with objectives, setup, conditions, fuels, publications and what varied between its tests. Every statement carries a word-for-word quote and a link to its source.
  • Methodology. How complete each condition and result is, where each value came from, how the numbers are computed, how the data was checked, how SI powers the dashboard, and its limits.

What the data shows

  • Of 1,872 individual tests, 20 were run inside the exploration atmosphere, and all 20 are gas-burner flames (ACME CFI-G).
  • No solid material, which is what actually burns in a habitat, was tested above 22.7 % oxygen. Every solid-fuel test that reports pressure was run at ISS cabin pressure, 98–104 kPa.
  • No test was run at real partial gravity. E-FIELD Flames only simulates it with an electric field.
  • For the ISS cabin, 154 of the 379 solid-fuel tests sit within 5 points of oxygen and 15 kPa of pressure. For a lunar or Mars habitat, none do.

How it works

  1. A Python pipeline calls the PSI API, downloads the metadata, the 22 experiment tables and the documents that explain their columns.
  2. Each table has a JSON mapping (which column feeds which field, in which unit, how to read special cells). Code applies the mapping to every row the same way and keeps the original cells and row number.
  3. When a table leaves a condition out but the same investigation records it in another NASA document, the value is taken from there, marked as such, and the document is quoted in the row's notes. Oxygen, pressure and airflow of the 121 BASS tests come from its As Run Test Matrix this way, and the pressure of 95 SAFFIRE and SAME-R tests is the median reading of each test's own sensor telemetry.
  4. The BASS table has no column for what happened in a test. A language model read the operators' free-text notes in NASA's As Run Test Matrix; code keeps the ignition, outcome or burn time it found only when the words it quotes are in the NASA cell character for character.
  5. Investigation cards are built from PSI metadata; code checks that every quote exists in the source text.
  6. The pipeline writes four JSON files that follow a published data contract and validates them.
  7. A static web app (Next.js, TypeScript) reads those files. Ranking, coverage and gaps are pure functions with unit tests that run in the browser: no server, no database.
  8. For each preset environment a language model wrote a short brief from the numbers the app computes. Each sentence lists the facts it rests on; the app re-checks every number and name against the data in the browser and does not show a sentence that fails. No model is called at run time.

How SI powers it, and how it is checked

SI reads and writes; ordinary code checks each result against its NASA source before it reaches a screen.

  • One table from 22. SI proposed how each NASA table maps onto the common fields and found conditions a table leaves out in other NASA files. A script compared over 2,100 converted oxygen, pressure and airflow values in 8 tables with their source cells: all match within 2 %.
  • Operator notes. SI read the 121 notes of the BASS operators and found the ignition of 113 tests, the outcome of 75 and the burn time of 17. A value is kept only when the quoted words are in the NASA cell: 205 kept, none rejected. The quote is shown beside the value.
  • SI brief. For each of the five preset environments SI wrote a short interpretation. Code checks every number and investigation name in it, in a unit test and again in the browser: 26 of 26 sentences pass, with 98 numbers and 24 names checked.
  • SI does not set or adjust a score, does not fill a value that no NASA file reports, and does not draw conclusions about how materials burn.
  • Everything SI produced is marked: an SI badge in the app, the model's name in the brief file and in the notes of each row it read, and a line in the footer of every demo slide.

What is creative about it

  • It answers with a scenario, not a search. The user describes an environment, and the tool brings the evidence to it and says how far each investigation is from it, part by part.
  • It treats "nobody tested this" as a result. The gaps are counted and drawn on the same grid as the tests, and every count opens the rows behind it.
  • SI works only where it can be checked. Every value it reads carries a word-for-word NASA quote, and every number it writes is checked again by code in the browser.

Benefits

  • Engineers and researchers get, in a minute, an answer that otherwise means reading 24 data pages and 352 publication records: which experiments are relevant to their environment, and which are not.
  • Modellers get one clean, documented table with units converted and the source of every value.
  • Mission planners see the gaps (oxygen-enriched low pressure, solid materials, partial gravity) before a habitat is designed around assumptions that were never tested.

Intended impact

Make the limits of existing microgravity fire data visible, so that the next flight experiments target the conditions crews will actually live in, and give modellers a trustworthy starting dataset.

What we considered

  • The users are researchers and engineers: a simple screen is fine, a wrong number is not. A value NASA does not report stays "not reported" and earns no points in the ranking.
  • Traceability: every value leads to its NASA file, row and original cell.
  • A table row is not always a test: rows that sum up a test day or a test-matrix range are marked and are not counted as tests.
  • Reproducibility: a static site with no server, no key and no model call at run time gives the same answer every time, and the code, the mappings and the data contract are open.

Tools, languages, software

Python (data pipeline: requests, openpyxl, python-docx, pdfplumber), TypeScript, Next.js with static export, React, Tailwind CSS, Vitest, ESLint, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages; Claude Code as the SI assistant. Details in the References field.

Data quality and limits

  • 1,989 rows from 22 tables; 1,872 are individual tests. Oxygen is reported for 1,479 tests, pressure for 1,258, airflow for 793, the outcome for 623. Missing values are shown as "not reported", never as zero.
  • Automated checks: over 2,100 oxygen, pressure and airflow values in 8 tables were compared with their source cells after unit conversion, and all match within 2 %. The site has 179 unit tests and the pipeline 44.
  • The ranking weights and the rules SI followed when reading the operators' notes are a first version.
  • The score compares test conditions; it is not a safety rating.
